passage:
On Saturday, Uday's football final ended in a draw, and his father's seat in the stands stayed empty. That night, when Uday asked why, Irfan snapped, "Some of us have real work!" and slammed the door of their Andheri flat.
Uday didn't come out for dinner.
On Sunday morning, Irfan knocked and sat on the edge of the bed. He didn't mention work or traffic.
"I promised to come and I didn't. Then I shouted at you for asking. Both were wrong. I'm sorry."
Uday kept looking at the ceiling. "You always say you'll come."
"You're right to be angry. I can't undo Saturday. Next Sunday's match, I've told my boss I'm off."
A long pause. Then Uday sat up. "The replay's on my phone. Want to see my header?"
Irfan leaned in. "Show me."

qa.q: Where did Irfan's seat stay empty?
qa.a: In the stands at Uday's football final.

qa.q: How was Uday feeling on Sunday morning, and what shows it?
qa.a: He was hurt and angry; he kept looking at the ceiling and said, "You always say you'll come."

qa.q: What made Irfan's apology a real repair?
qa.a: He named both mistakes, missing the match and shouting, apologised without excuses, accepted Uday's anger, and made a concrete change for next Sunday.

qa.q: What would change if Irfan had blamed work instead of apologising?
qa.a: Uday would likely stay shut in and learn that his hurt doesn't matter, instead of learning that the relationship can survive a mistake.

grounding: Shows a father who missed his son's match and shouted, then returns to name it and apologise without excuses, repairing the bond.

passage:
Dear Amandeep,
It's three years since we met in the hostel queue, and I wanted to write this down properly.
You know what home was like: some days warm, some days nobody spoke to me. So I grew up waiting for people to disappear. In first year, when you didn't reply for a day, I assumed you were done with me and stopped talking to you first.
But you kept turning up. Every Thursday, chai at the canteen, even when I was rude. When I cancelled, you just said, "Next Thursday, then." Slowly I stopped bracing.
My counsellor asked me last month what changed. I said, "Amandeep never disappeared." Now when someone goes quiet, I notice the old fear, and I ask instead of running.
Thank you for being boringly reliable. I mean that as the biggest compliment.
Tanvir

qa.q: What did Tanvir and Amandeep do every Thursday?
qa.a: They had chai at the canteen.

qa.q: How did Tanvir feel in first year when Amandeep didn't reply for a day?
qa.a: Tanvir felt insecure and afraid of being left, assuming Amandeep was done and pulling away first.

qa.q: What helped Tanvir become more secure?
qa.a: Amandeep's repeated reliability, plus talking with a counsellor and noticing the old fear, helped Tanvir ask instead of running.

qa.q: How might Amandeep feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Amandeep would likely feel touched and glad to learn that simply showing up every Thursday, even when Tanvir was rude, mattered so much.

grounding: Shows a young adult from an unpredictable home becoming more secure through a friend's steady reliability and reflection with a counsellor.

passage:
Nirmala, you keep saying "I'm just avoidant, that's how I am." Let your Shalini Aunty tell you something.
At twenty, I read an article about attachment styles and decided I was "avoidant". It felt like a relief, like a name for everything. When my friend Rupa was upset that I ignored her calls for a week, I said, "Sorry, that's my style." She stared at me and said, "Your style hurt me."
That stung. I went home and thought about it. With my grandmother I wasn't avoidant at all; I called her every day. With Rupa I pulled back only when she needed me.
So the label wasn't who I was. It helped me see why I pulled away. But I still owed Rupa an apology, and I gave her one, properly, at her doorstep, with her favourite sweets.
Use the idea to understand yourself, beta. Not as an excuse.

qa.q: Who did young Shalini call every day?
qa.a: Her grandmother.

qa.q: How did young Shalini feel when Rupa said "Your style hurt me"?
qa.a: She felt stung and ashamed, which made her go home and rethink using the label.

qa.q: What choice did young Shalini make after Rupa's words, and why was it wise?
qa.a: She took responsibility and apologised properly at Rupa's doorstep, instead of hiding behind the label.

qa.q: How did Rupa see the "that's my style" excuse?
qa.a: Rupa saw it as brushing off her hurt; a label didn't make being ignored for a week feel any better to her.

grounding: Shows an aunt recalling how she learned that an attachment style is a context-dependent tendency, not an identity or excuse, and still owned her behaviour.

passage:
Aditi had been staying with her sister Binita for two days when it happened again.
"You're checking your phone. Are you upset with me?" Binita asked.
"No," said Vikram, standing up. "I'm going to the balcony."
"See, you're leaving!"
"I'm leaving because you're following me!"
Later, Aditi found Binita in the kitchen. "Can I say what I'm seeing, Bini?"
"That he's cold?"
"That you chase when you're scared, and he hides when he's crowded. Then you chase harder, and he hides further. It's a circle. Nobody's the villain."
Binita was quiet. "It feels like his fault."
"I know. Maybe you could both look at the circle together? Even with a couples counsellor?"
That night, Aditi heard them on the balcony, talking quietly, for the first time that week.

qa.q: Where did Vikram go when Binita asked if he was upset?
qa.a: To the balcony.

qa.q: How did Aditi feel watching the argument, and what did she do with it?
qa.a: She was worried and wanted to help, so she gently asked Binita whether she could say what she was seeing.

qa.q: Why could seeing the pattern as a circle help Binita and Vikram?
qa.a: It stops them blaming one person and lets them notice together how chasing and hiding feed each other, which opens a way out.

qa.q: How might Vikram experience Binita's questions?
qa.a: Vikram seems to feel crowded when Binita follows him, so he pulls away to the balcony, even if he is not upset with her.

grounding: Shows a sister observing a couple's pursue-and-withdraw loop and naming it as a shared pattern rather than one person's fault.

Class teacher's note, Class 5, maths results day.
Rashmi usually beams at full marks and runs to show me. Today she got 14 out of 25. She folded the paper small and pushed it deep into her bag. When Samir got the top mark, she whispered, "I'm the stupid one now." At lunch she didn't eat, and told a friend, "My mother will be so disappointed in me."
I sat beside her: "One test shows what we need to practise. It doesn't show who you are." She shook her head, eyes wet.
Next: tomorrow I've asked Rashmi to help me set up the science corner, a job that has nothing to do with marks. This week I will call her mother to share how kind and hardworking Rashmi is, and talk about praising effort at home.

qa.q: What mark did Rashmi get on the maths test?
qa.a: 14 out of 25.

qa.q: How did Rashmi feel after seeing her mark?
qa.a: She felt ashamed and not good enough, calling herself "the stupid one" and worrying that her mother would be disappointed.

qa.q: What steps did the teacher plan to help Rashmi feel valued beyond marks?
qa.a: Giving her the science corner job, which has nothing to do with marks, and calling her mother to talk about Rashmi's kindness and praising effort at home.

qa.q: How might Samir's top mark look from Rashmi's side?
qa.a: To Rashmi it may feel like proof that she has lost her place, since her sense of worth depends on being the one with high marks.

grounding: Shows a teacher noticing a child whose worth depends on marks crumbling after one poor result, and planning ways to show she is valued.

passage:
When I was in Class 4, I entered the inter-school drawing contest and didn't win anything. I cried the whole way home.
Papa didn't say, "Next time you'll win." He looked at my drawing for a long time. Then he said, "You tried shading the clouds with your finger. That was clever. And you gave your extra crayons to Meenu when hers broke. I saw that."
I said, "But I lost." He said, "You tried something new. I'm proud of that."
After that I stopped only drawing things I knew I could do well. I tried faces, which are hard. Now I'm in Class 6, and I entered the contest again, with a face. I didn't win this time either. But I wasn't scared to try it, and Papa still says "tell me how you did the eyes" first.
Rekha

qa.q: What did Rekha give Meenu at the contest?
qa.a: Extra crayons, when Meenu's broke.

qa.q: How did Rekha feel on the way home from the first contest?
qa.a: Rekha felt sad and disappointed about losing, crying the whole way home.

qa.q: What did Papa praise, and how did it help Rekha?
qa.a: He praised trying finger-shading and giving crayons to Meenu, not the result, so Rekha stopped being scared of failing and started trying harder things like faces.

qa.q: What would change if Papa had only talked about winning next time?
qa.a: Rekha might have kept drawing only safe things, feeling worth depended on prizes, and been too scared to try faces.

grounding: Shows a father praising effort, strategy and kindness after a loss, so his child learns worth doesn't depend on winning and dares to try harder things.

passage:
At the climbing wall in a Madrid sports centre, Sofia stood at the back of her PE group with her arms crossed. "This is for babies," she announced. When Lucía slipped off the second hold, Sofia laughed loudest.
Her turn came. "I'm not doing it. It's boring." Her hands, though, were shaking inside her sleeves.
The coach, Dalia, didn't argue. After class, when the hall was empty, she said, "Want to try the easy wall? No one's watching. Falling off is part of it."
Sofia hesitated, then climbed three holds and slid off onto the mat. Her face went red. She waited for Dalia to laugh.
Dalia only said, "Your left foot was good. Again?"
Sofia tried again. This time she reached the fifth hold.

qa.q: How many holds did Sofia climb the second time?
qa.a: She reached the fifth hold.

qa.q: What might Sofia have been afraid of when she called climbing boring?
qa.a: She seemed scared of failing in front of the others; her hands were shaking inside her sleeves even while she acted confident.

qa.q: Why did Dalia's offer work better than a lecture?
qa.a: She gave Sofia a private, safe chance to fail with no one watching, and answered the fall with specific praise instead of mockery.

qa.q: What might it have been like for Lucía when Sofia laughed loudest?
qa.a: Lucía probably felt embarrassed and hurt, slipping in front of everyone and being mocked for it.

grounding: Shows a teen whose boasting and mocking cover a fear of being seen failing, and how a safe chance to fail helps more than a lecture.

passage:
At midnight in his room in Mexico City, Alejandro was still scrolling a photo app. Boys his age on beaches, with sharp jawlines and hundreds of likes. His own post from the morning had eleven. He deleted it.
He checked again at breakfast. Nothing new. His chest felt heavy all day.
On Saturday his friend Kofi turned up with a bag of spanners. "The bike, remember? You promised."
They spent the afternoon fixing the old bicycle in the courtyard, hands black with grease. Kofi's little brother cheered when the chain finally caught.
That evening Alejandro rode it round the block twice. He didn't take a single photo. He noticed, falling asleep, that he hadn't opened the app all day, and that the day had felt good anyway.

qa.q: How many likes did Alejandro's morning post have?
qa.a: Eleven.

qa.q: How did Alejandro feel after deleting his post?
qa.a: He felt behind and low; his chest felt heavy all day and he kept checking for likes.

qa.q: What gave Alejandro firmer ground than likes?
qa.a: Fixing the bike with Kofi and riding it gave him a real achievement and friendship, which felt good without being posted.

qa.q: How might Kofi see that Saturday?
qa.a: To Kofi it was just keeping a promise and having fun fixing the bike; he may not know how much the afternoon lifted Alejandro.

grounding: Shows a teen whose self-worth rises and falls with likes finding firmer ground in an offline project with a friend.

passage:
In the school study hall, Sharmila crumpled another page. "I'm so stupid. I can't even write a paragraph."
Wasim looked up. It was the fourth time that week he'd heard her say it. On Monday she had turned down the chance to read her poem in assembly: "They'll laugh."
He leaned over. "Can I be honest? Your poem about your grandmother's hands is the best thing anyone wrote this term. The line about the turmeric stains, I still remember it."
Sharmila stared at the table. "You're just being nice."
"I'm being specific." He didn't leave. He sat with her till the bell.
As they packed up, he said quietly, "You've seemed down for weeks. Would you talk to Mrs Das? I'll come along."
She nodded. They walked to the staff room together, and Mrs Das made time to see her that afternoon.

qa.q: What did Sharmila turn down on Monday?
qa.a: The chance to read her poem in assembly.

qa.q: How did Wasim feel hearing Sharmila call herself stupid again?
qa.a: He was concerned, since it was the fourth time that week, and he chose to stay and offer honest praise.

qa.q: What did Wasim do that a good friend could copy?
qa.a: He gave specific, honest praise, stayed close until the bell, and gently encouraged her to talk to a trusted adult, even offering to go with her.

qa.q: Why might Sharmila say "You're just being nice"?
qa.a: Her low sense of worth makes praise hard to believe, so kind words feel fake to her, even specific ones.

grounding: Shows a friend who hears repeated put-downs, offers honest specific praise, stays close, and helps her reach a trusted adult.

passage:
Monday: Before her internship interview, Devika sent photos of three kurtas to six friends. When Anand replied, "The blue is a bit dull," her stomach dropped. She changed twice and nearly cried.
Thursday: Choosing her final-year project topic, she reached for her phone to ask the group. She stopped and put it face down. Instead she wrote three reasons she liked the topic on urban gardens, in her own words, and chose it.
Two weeks later: Her professor said, "Your introduction is weak." The old sting came back, hot and fast. She wanted to message five people for comfort. She opened her notebook to the three reasons instead, read them twice, and started rewriting the introduction. By evening she felt steadier, even a little proud.

qa.q: How many friends did Devika send kurta photos to?
qa.a: Six friends.

qa.q: How did Devika feel when Anand said the blue was a bit dull?
qa.a: She felt crushed and anxious; her stomach dropped, she changed twice and nearly cried.

qa.q: What did Devika do on Thursday that started building her own sense of worth?
qa.a: She put the phone face down and wrote her own three reasons for the topic, choosing it without asking the group.

qa.q: What would change if Devika had messaged five people after the professor's comment?
qa.a: She might have felt better briefly, but the comfort would fade, and she would miss the chance to steady herself with her own reasons.

grounding: Shows a young adult who seeks opinions before every choice and is crushed by mild criticism, slowly building an inner sense of worth.
